Django was first released in July 2005, drawn out of a newspaper's websites (`docs/releases/1.0.txt`, `docs/faq/general.txt`; [Where Django came from, and who makes it](../introduction/origins.md)).

Django 0.95, released in 2006, chiefly merged a branch called magic-removal, which removed constraints on how code had to be written that "were a consequence of decisions made in the early days of Django, prior to its open-source release" (`docs/releases/0.95.txt`).

After it, models stayed in the module that defined them, a model overrode `Model.save` and `Model.delete` as any class overrides a method, and custom table-level functions went on a new Manager API (`django/db/models/manager.py:BaseManager`).

Pieces of the framework, the template system for one, could be configured without an environment variable, to be used inside other applications, as `LazySettings.configure` allows now (`django/conf/__init__.py:LazySettings.configure`).
And Django no longer required a database: a project that defines none gets a `"default"` on the dummy backend, which raises when used (`django/db/utils.py:ConnectionHandler.configure_settings`).

`Model._meta` dates from the magic-removal too, say the 1.8 notes, and became an official API only in 1.8 (`docs/releases/1.8.txt`; [The options: what a model keeps as `_meta`](../models/options.md)).

0.96 shipped its replacement beside it as django.newforms, copied the old one to django.oldforms, and set the schedule: the next release would move newforms to django.forms, and the one after would remove oldforms (`docs/releases/0.96.txt`).

Django 1.0, [released in September 2008](https://www.djangoproject.com/weblog/2008/sep/03/1/), made the move and rebuilt the admin on the new forms, with admin definitions "completely decoupled from model definitions (no more class Admin declaration in models!)"; the helpers form_for_model and form_for_instance gave way to `ModelForm` (`docs/releases/1.0.txt`).

A model's admin options live outside it, on a `ModelAdmin`, which is registered for the model with `AdminSite.register` and builds a `ModelForm` for it (`django/contrib/admin/sites.py:AdminSite.register`, `django/contrib/admin/options.py:ModelAdmin.get_form`; [Registering models: `AdminSite.register` and `ModelAdmin`](../admin/registration.md)).

A model's admin options live outside it, on a `ModelAdmin`, which is registered for the model with `AdminSite.register` and builds a `ModelForm` for it (`django/contrib/admin/sites.py:AdminSite.register`, `django/contrib/admin/options.py:ModelAdmin.get_form`; [Registering models: `AdminSite.register` and `ModelAdmin`](../admin/registration.md)).

The form helpers had been deprecated before 1.0 removed them; by 1.2 a deprecated feature raised a `PendingDeprecationWarning`, silent by default, then a `DeprecationWarning` in the next release, and went in the third (`docs/releases/1.0.txt`, `docs/releases/1.2.txt`; [What changed](../changes.md#how-a-change-is-carried)).

The form helpers had been deprecated before 1.0 removed them; by 1.2 a deprecated feature raised a `PendingDeprecationWarning`, silent by default, then a `DeprecationWarning` in the next release, and went in the third (`docs/releases/1.0.txt`, `docs/releases/1.2.txt`; [What changed](../changes.md#how-a-change-is-carried)).
1.2 replaced them with `DATABASES`, connections by alias with one named `"default"` (`docs/releases/1.2.txt`).
Both keep those signatures (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.get_db_prep_value`).
1.3 configured caches "in the same way", by alias in `CACHES` (`docs/releases/1.3.txt`).

`ConnectionHandler` and `CacheHandler` are now both subclasses of `BaseConnectionHandler` (`django/utils/connection.py:BaseConnectionHandler`; [Connections by alias: `DATABASES` and `ConnectionHandler`](../backends/connections.md)).

1.3, in 2011, added class-based views, so that a view could be composed "out of a collection of methods that can be subclassed and overridden", and deprecated the functions, which 1.5 removed (`docs/releases/1.3.txt`, `docs/internals/deprecation.txt`).

1.3, in 2011, added class-based views, so that a view could be composed "out of a collection of methods that can be subclassed and overridden", and deprecated the functions, which 1.5 removed (`docs/releases/1.3.txt`, `docs/internals/deprecation.txt`).

The URLconf did not change for them: since 0.96 a pattern could name any callable, where before it named a string (`docs/releases/0.96.txt`), and a class-based view enters it as the function `View.as_view` returns (`django/views/generic/base.py:View.as_view`; [`View.as_view` and dispatch](../views/as-view.md)).

Django had used naive datetimes, "leaving it up to each developer to interpret what a given date/time 'really means'"; 1.4, in 2012, added a mode that stores datetimes in UTC, works with aware ones and converts them to the user's time zone in templates and forms, and startproject turned it on (`docs/releases/1.4.txt`).

The settings startproject writes still set `USE_TZ`, true by default only since 5.0 (`docs/releases/5.0.txt`, `django/conf/project_template/project_name/settings.py-tpl`; [Time zones](../i18n/time-zones.md)).

The settings startproject writes still set `USE_TZ`, true by default only since 5.0 (`docs/releases/5.0.txt`, `django/conf/project_template/project_name/settings.py-tpl`; [Time zones](../i18n/time-zones.md)).

1.4 also moved manage.py out of the project package, where its handling of import paths could import a module twice, and added `wsgi.py`, whose application the development server runs too, named by `WSGI_APPLICATION` (`docs/releases/1.4.txt`).

Since 1.7 that fails with `AppRegistryNotReady`: the registry of the installed applications and their models is filled by `django.setup`, and it is `get_wsgi_application` that calls `django.setup` (`docs/releases/1.7.txt`, `django/core/wsgi.py:get_wsgi_application`; [The two entry points](../handlers/entry.md)).

1.5, in 2013, was "the first release with Python 3 support", one codebase for both Pythons, called experimental; 1.6 supported Python 3 officially (`docs/releases/1.5.txt`, `docs/releases/1.6.txt`).

Python 2 stayed into the second decade, and loaddata still opens fixtures in binary mode, a choice its comment says may be revisited after dropping Python 2 (`django/core/management/commands/loaddata.py:Command.compression_formats`).
1.5 also let a project replace the user model, and deprecated AUTH_PROFILE_MODULE, the setting that had named a profile model for extra data (`docs/releases/1.5.txt`).

`User` declares itself swappable for `AUTH_USER_MODEL`, `Options.swapped` names the model that replaces it, and code asks `get_user_model` for the one in use (`django/db/models/options.py:Options.swapped`, `django/contrib/auth/__init__.py:get_user_model`; [The user model: `AbstractBaseUser`, `User` and `AUTH_USER_MODEL`](../auth/user-model.md)).

Until 1.6, in 2013, the database's own autocommit was off by default, and transactions were managed through TransactionMiddleware and decorators such as commit_on_success and commit_manually (`docs/releases/1.6.txt`, `docs/releases/1.3.txt`).

1.6 turned the database's autocommit on by default and deprecated those APIs, which 1.8 removed (`docs/releases/1.6.txt`, `docs/internals/deprecation.txt`).

What stands now is `atomic`, a block that commits or rolls back and nests as savepoints (`django/db/transaction.py:Atomic`; [Transactions: autocommit, `atomic` and savepoints](../backends/transactions.md)), and a database's `"ATOMIC_REQUESTS"`, which, when true, wraps a view in one (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler.make_view_atomic`).

A `TestCase`'s tests had run in a transaction rolled back after each since 1.1 (`docs/releases/1.1.txt`); 1.8 rebuilt `TestCase` on `atomic`, one block for the class, where `TestCase.setUpTestData` runs, and one for each test (`docs/releases/1.8.txt`, `django/test/testcases.py:TestCase._enter_atomics`; [A transaction around each test: `TestCase`](../testing/test-case.md)).

1.7, in 2014, replaced it with the app registry: an application is an `AppConfig`, which may run code at startup in `AppConfig.ready`, and every application and model is imported as Django starts (`docs/releases/1.7.txt`).
That is `Apps.populate`, which `django.setup` calls (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.populate`; [Populating the app registry](../startup/populate.md)).

`Options.get_field` still uses the old name: asked for a field it cannot find among its own while the models are not ready, it says that the app cache isn't ready (`django/db/models/options.py:Options.get_field`).

The same release built in schema migrations: syncdb gave way to migrate, makemigrations writes migration files from the models, and every field must describe itself for those files through a new required method, `Field.deconstruct` (`docs/releases/1.7.txt`, `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.deconstruct`; [Migrations](../migrations.md)). syncdb survives inside migrate: with `--run-syncdb`, `Command.sync_apps` creates the tables of applications without migrations, and a test database is made with that option (`django/core/management/commands/migrate.py:Command.sync_apps`; [The migrate command, showmigrations and sqlmigrate](../migrations/migrate.md)).

The 1.7 notes do not name South, [a third-party migrations application](https://www.djangoproject.com/weblog/2014/sep/02/release-17-final/); a comment does, where `MigrationQuestioner.ask_initial` looks for Python files in a migrations package before offering a first migration, to pass over South's (`django/db/migrations/questioner.py:MigrationQuestioner.ask_initial`).

In 2014 Django adopted a process for proposals, DEP 1, a near-copy of Python's PEPs (`deps:final/0001-dep-process.rst`; [Where Django came from, and who makes it](../introduction/origins.md#django-enhancement-proposals)).
1.1 had added aggregates, `QuerySet.aggregate` and `QuerySet.annotate`, and `F`, a reference to another field (`docs/releases/1.1.txt`).

By 2014, as DEP 181 by Anssi Kääriäinen describes, an `F` expression was turned into SQL by a private, global SQLEvaluator that had to know every kind of node, and aggregates were not expressions at all, so two could not be added to each other; annotate took nothing but aggregates (`deps:final/0181-orm-expressions.rst`).

An expression is bound to a query by `BaseExpression.resolve_expression` and writes its SQL with `BaseExpression.as_sql`; an `Aggregate` is a `Func` like any database function; and `F`, as the DEP proposed, is not an expression but resolves to one (`django/db/models/aggregates.py:Aggregate`, `django/db/models/expressions.py:F.resolve_expression`; [Expressions: `resolve_expression` and `as_sql`](../sql/expressions.md)).

An expression is bound to a query by `BaseExpression.resolve_expression` and writes its SQL with `BaseExpression.as_sql`; an `Aggregate` is a `Func` like any database function; and `F`, as the DEP proposed, is not an expression but resolves to one (`django/db/models/aggregates.py:Aggregate`, `django/db/models/expressions.py:F.resolve_expression`; [Expressions: `resolve_expression` and `as_sql`](../sql/expressions.md)).

`SQLCompiler.compile` calls such a method in place of `as_sql` where an expression has one, and Django's own expressions define such methods for its built-in backends, as `Value.as_sqlite` does (`django/db/models/sql/compiler.py:SQLCompiler.compile`, `django/db/models/expressions.py:Value.as_sqlite`).

`SQLCompiler.compile` calls such a method in place of `as_sql` where an expression has one, and Django's own expressions define such methods for its built-in backends, as `Value.as_sqlite` does (`django/db/models/sql/compiler.py:SQLCompiler.compile`, `django/db/models/expressions.py:Value.as_sqlite`).

DEP 182, by Aymeric Augustin, gave convenience and speed as reasons users were turning to other engines, Jinja2 above all, and proposed a stable API for template backends, with Jinja2 built in and the Django template language kept as the default (`deps:final/0182-multiple-template-engines.rst`).

`TEMPLATES` lists the engines, each a backend class named by its `"BACKEND"`, and `get_template` asks them in order until one finds the template (`django/template/loader.py:get_template`; [Template engines: `TEMPLATES` and the backends](../templates/engines.md)).

Since users would have to write the new setting, the DEP proposed moving the context processors too, out of django.core, where, the DEP recalls, the magic-removal had left them; 1.8 put them in `django.template.context_processors` (`deps:final/0182-multiple-template-engines.rst`, `docs/releases/1.8.txt`).

Since users would have to write the new setting, the DEP proposed moving the context processors too, out of django.core, where, the DEP recalls, the magic-removal had left them; 1.8 put them in `django.template.context_processors` (`deps:final/0182-multiple-template-engines.rst`, `docs/releases/1.8.txt`).

It chose the last, keeping the first for atypical cases, and so `TEMPLATES` is a list, where `DATABASES` and `CACHES` are dictionaries: its order decides which engine wins, so a project can put replacements for an application's templates first (`deps:final/0182-multiple-template-engines.rst`).

The proposals went on after 1.8: the new middleware of 1.10 was DEP 5's, and asynchronous Django is DEP 9's (`docs/releases/1.10.txt`, `deps:accepted/0009-async.rst`), both told in [The second decade: from 1.9 to 5.0](second-decade.md).
